summary: Outlines the process by which the IETF selects an appointment to the Internet Society (ISOC) Board of Trustees. It is a best current practice document about community governance rather than a technical protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3677 explains how the IETF picks the person it sends to sit on the Internet Society's Board of Trustees. The Internet Architecture Board asks for nominations each January, reviews them and chooses a candidate, and the Internet Engineering Steering Group then confirms that choice. New trustees start their three-year term at the Internet Society's annual meeting in June.

subtitle: How the IETF chooses the person it nominates to the Internet Society's Board of Trustees each year.

tldr.problem: The IETF has to name one trustee each year to the Internet Society's Board of Trustees, and it had no written process for choosing that person.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB calls for nominations on a public mailing list, reviews them and selects a candidate, and the IESG confirms the choice, all inside a three-stage schedule that ends before the Internet Society's June annual meeting.
tldr.outcome: The document is a Best Current Practice, not a protocol. It also covers filling a trustee seat early if the sitting trustee cannot serve the full term.

today: RFC 3677 is a Best Current Practice published in December 2003, and it has not been obsoleted or updated. It describes a governance process rather than a protocol, so nothing on the network depends on it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet Society (ISOC) provides organizational and financial support for the IETF. As the ISOC by-laws stipulate, the IETF is called upon to name 3 Trustees to the ISOC Board of Trustees (BoT), with staggered 3 year terms. That arrangement means the IETF names one Trustee each year.

This memo sets out the process the IETF follows to make that selection. It also covers the mid-term vacancies that may arise with IETF-nominated Board positions. In short, the document describes the timeframe and the procedures for the IAB to solicit public input and make a selection for the open position each year.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF names three people to sit on the Internet Society's Board of Trustees. Their terms last three years and are staggered, so one new trustee is chosen each year. This document describes how that choice is made.

sections.title: Why the IAB Makes the Selection
sections.content:
An alternative approach would be to use the IETF's Nominating Committee (NomCom), described in RFC 2727 and its revisions. The memo says NomCom is chartered and defined specifically for selecting people for IETF organization tasks, and that the ISOC Board appointment does not fit that in two ways. First, the timeframe of the appointment does not mesh with the IETF appointment cycle. Second, the nature of the deliberations and the type of information solicited would be significantly different for an external appointment, such as this appointment to the ISOC Board.

The memo says the first issue, timing, could be resolved fairly easily for this specific appointment. The second issue is more general, and is not reasonably reconciled with the IETF NomCom task as currently specified. The process described in RFC 2727 is oriented toward soliciting feedback from the IETF community about individuals and technical positions with which they have personal experience. To make a good decision on external appointments, the NomCom would have to understand the requirements of those positions and evaluate candidates for a very different set of skills than IAB and IESG members need. It might also have to ask for feedback from outside the IETF community.

The memo is careful to note that the people who make up the IETF NomCom each year have the competence to carry out such a search. The issue, it says, is that it is a very different task, would take additional time and resources, and is therefore a side effort that could well undermine the effectiveness of the NomCom in its primary task for the IETF.

By contrast, the IAB is chartered to be responsible for IETF external liaisons, is a standing body that works with ISOC and the ISOC Board, and therefore has a working knowledge of the requirements of the specific position discussed here. The memo proposes that broadening the scope of the IETF NomCom role, or creating a separate nominating committee for such external non-liaison appointments, is not necessary or desirable for the purposes of this one annual appointment.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF already has a nominating committee for filling IETF jobs, but this document does not use it. Picking an outside trustee needs different skills and a different timetable, and the IAB already works with the Internet Society, so it makes the choice itself.

sections.title: Qualifications for an IETF-Nominated Trustee
sections.content:
Candidates for an ISOC Trustee should have a demonstrable involvement in the IETF, with a particular focus on active participation in IETF Working Groups. The candidate is expected to possess clearly demonstrated technical competence in Internet technology, and to be able to articulate technology issues such that the ISOC Board can be provided with sound technical perspectives.

The candidate is also expected to understand the respective roles and responsibilities of the IETF and ISOC, and to be able to articulate those roles within both organizational communities. The candidate will also be expected to exercise all the duties of an ISOC Board member: fiduciary responsibility, setting of policies, oversight of the operation of the Society, representing the interests of the members and stakeholders of the Society, and participation in all Board meetings and Board activity programs.

The candidate is not a representative or a delegate of the IETF, and is not chartered to represent the IETF or the IETF Standards Process within the ISOC Board or the broader ISOC community. The memo does expect the candidate to be able to call on experts in the IETF community as required, to ensure that the ISOC Board receives the highest quality technical advice available.
sections.plainLanguage: The person nominated should have worked in IETF working groups, be technically strong in Internet technology, and understand how the IETF and the Internet Society differ in role. They would sit on the board as an individual, not as a spokesperson for the IETF.

sections.title: Nominations and Eligibility
sections.content:
Each year the IAB makes a public call for nominations on the ietf-announce@ietf.org mailing list. The public call specifies the manner in which nominations will be accepted and the means by which the list of nominees will be published. Self-nominations are permitted.

Along with the name and contact information for each candidate, details about the candidate's background and qualifications for the position should be attached to the nomination. All IETF participants are eligible for nomination, including working group chairs, IETF NomCom members, IAB members and IESG members.

IAB and IESG members who accept nomination recuse themselves from the selection discussions and from the confirmation discussions respectively.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone in the IETF community can put themselves forward, including working group chairs and IAB or IESG members. The IAB asks for names on a public mailing list, and members who accept a nomination step back from deciding it.

sections.title: Selection and Confirmation
sections.content:
The IAB publishes the list of nominated persons, reviews the nomination material, and makes a selection. The selection criteria include additional consideration of any nominated candidates who are concurrently members of the IAB or the IESG, such that at the time of selection no more than two of the three IETF-appointed ISOC Trustees are IAB and IESG members.

The IESG acts as the confirming body for the selection. In the event that the IESG determines not to confirm the nominated candidate, the IESG provides the IAB with the basis for that determination, and the IAB nominates another candidate.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB reads the nominations and picks one candidate. At most two of the three IETF trustees may also be IAB or IESG members. The IESG then checks the choice, and if it says no, the IAB has to find someone else.

sections.title: The Annual Timeframe
sections.content:
ISOC expects to seat new Board members at its annual general meeting in June of each year. The memo sets out three basic timeframe requirements for the IETF process: 4-6 weeks for the solicitation of nominations, 4-6 weeks for the review of nominees, deliberation and selection, and 4-6 weeks for confirmation, including re-selection as necessary, and delivery to ISOC.

In January of each year the IAB announces the specific dates for that year's IETF ISOC Trustee selection process, taking into account the particular dates of the first IETF meeting of the year, and following the guidelines above.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet Society seats new board members at its June meeting, so the work happens in three stages of four to six weeks each: collecting nominations, choosing a candidate, and confirming the choice and handing the name over. The IAB publishes the exact dates each January.

sections.title: Mid-Term Vacancies
sections.content:
The document describes the process for the general, annual appointment of ISOC Trustees to fill the seats of trustees whose terms are ending. If an IETF-appointed trustee is unable to serve the full term, the IAB may, at its discretion, immediately select a replacement to serve the remainder of the term, using the interim process defined in section 3.5.1. If the IAB does not invoke the interim process, the next annual selection process fills the vacancy, if the vacant term does not end at that point, as well as the regular appointment for that selection cycle.

If the IAB elects to fill the mid-term vacancy before the next annual selection, a separate timeline is announced and the rest of the process described in this document is followed.
sections.plainLanguage: If a trustee leaves early, the IAB can either pick a replacement straight away, on a timetable it announces, or leave the seat empty until the next annual round, which then fills both the gap and the regular position.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it does not describe any technical protocols and has no implications for network security.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing here describes a network protocol, so this document has no effect on network security.
